title: Guidelines for Writing RFC Text on Security Considerations
summary: Gives guidelines to RFC authors on how to write a good Security Considerations section, which every RFC must have. It notes that these sections have often been weak and suggests what to cover. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Every rulebook should warn about what can go wrong. This memo coaches authors on how to write those warnings well.

questions: how to write a security considerations section
what is the difference between passive and active attacks
what attacks must an rfc consider
subtitle: A tutorial on security terms and attacks, plus the rules for writing a Security Considerations section in an RFC.

tldr.problem: Every RFC must have a Security Considerations section, but such sections have historically been relatively weak.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the goals of security, sets out the Internet threat model and common attacks, explains common issues like authentication and denial of service, and says what authors MUST cover.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 72) that tells authors to state which attacks are in and out of scope and, for in-scope attacks, whether the protocol is susceptible or protected.

today: RFC 3552 is a Best Current Practice. It has been updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 9416.

sections.title: Purpose and Structure
sections.content:
RFC 2223 requires all RFCs to contain a Security Considerations section. The aim is both to encourage authors to think about security in their designs and to inform readers of the relevant issues. This memo gives authors guidance toward both ends.

It has three parts: a security tutorial that also defines common terms, a series of guidelines for writing the section, and a series of examples. It uses the key words from RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: Every rulebook has to include a part about dangers. This guide teaches authors how to write that part well.

sections.title: The Goals of Security
sections.content:
Security is not one property but a series of related, somewhat independent ones, and not all are needed for every application. The RFC divides them into communication security (protecting communications) and system security (protecting systems).

Communication security has three goals. Confidentiality keeps data secret from unintended listeners. Data integrity means the receiver gets the data the sender sent. Peer entity authentication means you know an endpoint is the one you intended; in messaging this is called data origin authentication. Without it, confidentiality and integrity are hard to provide. A fourth property, non-repudiation, is the ability to demonstrate to a third party who sent a message. The RFC notes it can be very difficult to achieve and that naive approaches are generally inadequate.

System security covers unauthorized usage (use by people who are not permitted), inappropriate usage (actions forbidden even to authorized users, such as sending files that contain viruses) and denial of service (attacks that deprive legitimate users of resources, often easy to mount and hard to stop).
sections.eli5: Being safe means several things: nobody peeks at your letter, nobody changes it, you know who sent it, and the mailbox stays open for you to use.

sections.title: The Internet Threat Model
sections.content:
A threat model describes what an attacker is assumed able to do. It has two jobs: identify the threats you care about and explicitly rule some out of scope.

For the Internet, the RFC assumes the end systems have not been compromised, but that the attacker has nearly complete control of the communications channel. The attacker can read any protocol data unit (PDU) and undetectably remove, change or inject forged packets, including packets that appear to come from a trusted machine.

Not every attacker has that much power. A passive attack only reads packets, as in sniffing a password off the wire. An active attack writes to the network. The RFC also separates on-path attackers, who sit on the route and can read, modify or remove datagrams, from off-path attackers, who can send forged datagrams but cannot necessarily receive replies. Designers MUST NOT assume that all attackers will be off-path, but are expected to give more weight to attacks that off-path attackers can also mount.

On a link, a protocol can require the IP TTL to be set to 255 and check it on receipt, which gives some reason to believe the packet came from the same link. This needs care with tunneling systems that may not decrement TTL.
sections.eli5: To plan for burglars you must decide what a burglar can do. Here the guide assumes the attacker controls the road between you and your friend, though not your house.

sections.title: Common Attack Patterns
sections.content:
The RFC lists attack patterns that can be adapted to almost any protocol.

  • Passive: confidentiality violations, password sniffing of reusable passwords sent in the clear, and offline cryptographic attacks such as a dictionary attack on a captured challenge-response pair.
  • Replay: recording messages and playing them back, even without understanding them. A replayed S/MIME purchase request could execute twice.
  • Message insertion: injecting a forged message, as a flood of spurious TCP SYN packets does by filling half-open connection tables.
  • Message deletion: removing a message from the wire.
  • Message modification: removing, changing and reinjecting a message, including cut-and-paste attacks.
  • Man-in-the-middle: the attacker poses as each side to the other. It attacks the identity of the parties, so integrity protection alone is insufficient. It is possible whenever a protocol lacks peer entity authentication, though authenticating just one side is enough to prevent it.

The RFC advises always using message authentication when you use encryption, to avoid cut-and-paste attacks such as the one it describes against IPsec ESP used without a MAC.
sections.eli5: Attackers can listen in, copy and resend a note, sneak in a fake note, throw one away, scribble on one, or pretend to be your friend to you and you to your friend.

sections.title: Common Issues in Protocol Security
sections.content:
User authentication. Plaintext username/password systems are not acceptable in IETF standards and can be mitigated by running over an encrypted connection such as TLS or IPsec. One-time passwords and challenge-response resist replay but can fall to offline keysearch or dictionary attacks. Other options are shared keys, key distribution centers (Kerberos is the most popular) and certificates, which bind an identity to a public key and rely on trusted roots established out of band. For host authentication, the certificate must be securely bound to the expected hostname.

Authorization is not authentication. Authentication identifies a party; authorization decides whether that party may perform an action, for instance through access control lists.

Traffic security. Protocols can be secured themselves or run over a channel security system. IPsec can protect all traffic between two hosts but is hard to deploy, and designers MUST NOT assume it will be available. TLS runs over a reliable transport such as TCP, cannot secure UDP, and does not stop forged TCP RST attacks. Using a separate port or negotiating upward to TLS both need care so an attacker cannot force a clear connection. Generic frameworks like SASL and GSS-API are open to downgrade attacks.

Denial of service. Authors of Internet standards MUST describe which denial of service attacks their protocol is susceptible to, and why avoiding them was unreasonable or out of scope. Two common defenses are making the attacker do more work than you do, and making the attacker prove they can receive data from you, as Photuris does with a cookie. TCP SYN floods are the standing example of a blind attack.

Object versus channel security and firewalls round out the list. Channel security such as TLS protects mail only in transit, whereas object security such as S/MIME protects the message itself. Designers cannot safely assume a walled garden behind a firewall.
sections.eli5: There are known tools for each problem: secret handshakes to prove who you are, locks on the road, and tricks that make pests do more work than you do. Each tool has weak spots to know about.

sections.title: Writing a Security Considerations Section
sections.content:
A protocol does not have to be immune to every attack, but authors must consider as many as possible. Authors MUST describe which attacks are out of scope (and why), which are in scope, and, for those, whether the protocol is susceptible or protects against them.

At least these attacks MUST be considered: eavesdropping, replay, message insertion, deletion, modification and man-in-the-middle. Potential denial of service attacks MUST be identified. If the protocol uses cryptography, the text should say which data is protected and how, and label secret data such as keying material. If it involves authentication, authors MUST document the assumptions that its security rests on.

It is insufficient to say a protocol should be run over some lower-layer security protocol. The protections expected from it MUST be specified, along with the properties of the combined system. The IESG will in general not approve standards track protocols that lack strong authentication, whether internal or through tight binding to a lower layer.

The threat environment MUST at a minimum include deployment across the global Internet over multiple administrative boundaries, without assuming firewalls. The section should also describe residual risk after mitigation and the risks of misapplying the protocol.
sections.eli5: The rules say: list every danger you thought of, say which ones your rules handle and which they do not, and never assume a safe fence around everyone.

sections.title: Worked Examples: SMTP and VRRP
sections.content:
The first example revisits SMTP. RFC 821 had no Security Considerations section, and RFC 2821 added a detailed one. The RFC reproduces that section with its own NOTE comments and new sections. It stresses that SMTP mail cannot be authenticated, and that integrity cannot be provided, at the transport level, so real mail security lies in end-to-end methods using digital signatures, such as PGP or S/MIME. New sections cover inappropriate usage, communications security (IPsec, TLS, S/MIME and PGP/MIME) and denial of service.

The second example is the security considerations of VRRP, presented as a good section clipped from a current protocol. It includes a TTL=255 check on receipt, and discusses three authentication types: none, simple text password and IP Authentication Header.
sections.eli5: The guide ends with two sample danger lists, one for email and one for a router-sharing protocol, so authors can see what a good one looks like.

sections.title: Its Own Security Section
sections.content: The Security Considerations section of this RFC consists of one sentence: this entire document is about security considerations. It is a guideline document and defines no protocol, so there is nothing further for it to analyze.
sections.eli5: The guide's own danger section says the whole guide is about dangers, so there is nothing more to add.
